lesson.title: SSID: Naming a Network You Cannot See
lesson.summary: An SSID is the human-readable name a Wi-Fi network broadcasts so people and devices can find and choose it, but it functions purely as a label and provides no security on its own.
lesson.body:
Open a phone's Wi-Fi settings in any coffee shop or apartment building, and a list of network names appears: things like CoffeeShop_Guest or NETGEAR34. A wireless signal is invisible and, unlike a cable, is not obviously tied to any particular business or household, so wireless LANs need some human-readable way to distinguish one network from the dozens of others that might be in radio range at the same physical location. That label is the SSID, Service Set Identifier, a name of up to 32 bytes that an access point attaches to the network it creates.

The access point advertises its SSID by sending beacon frames, small broadcast messages transmitted roughly ten times a second, that announce the network's presence, its SSID, its supported data rates, and its security settings. A client device scanning for networks listens for these beacons and presents the SSIDs it hears to the user, which is exactly the list that shows up in a phone's Wi-Fi settings screen. An access point can also be configured to omit its SSID from beacon frames, often called a hidden network, but the SSID is still transmitted in other frame types whenever a client actively connects, so hiding it mainly removes it from casual browsing lists rather than providing real security.

It helps to be precise about what an SSID is not. It is an identifier, comparable to a name tag, not a password or an encryption key. Two different networks in the same building can technically use the identical SSID, which confuses users but breaks no protocol rule; a network's actual security comes from separate mechanisms, primarily WPA encryption and authentication, layered on top of, not derived from, the SSID string. A single access point can also broadcast more than one SSID at once, for example a household router presenting one SSID for trusted family devices and a second, separate SSID for guests, each one appearing as its own distinct network in a device's list even though the same physical radio and the same physical access point are serving both.

Imagine a university library where the IT department deploys dozens of access points across four floors, and every single one is configured with the same SSID, Library-WiFi. A student's laptop sees only one entry, Library-WiFi, in its network list, not forty separate entries for forty separate APs, because the SSID's whole purpose is to represent one logical network to the user even when many physical access points cooperate underneath it. That cooperation, many access points sharing one SSID and letting a client roam between them, is precisely what the BSS and ESS concepts describe structurally.

Because the SSID is the identifier a client actually associates with when it joins a Wi-Fi network, it becomes one of the two building blocks, alongside the access point itself, that define a basic service set, the fundamental unit of Wi-Fi network structure covered next.
